title: Evaluating Generate–Validate–Repair Pipelines for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study comparing a baseline single‑shot LLM configuration generator against a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline (with a canary stage) on a 1000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus (2000 paired episodes). The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses) and validation used a deterministic digital‑twin validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics exactly one sampled initial generation per task was deterministically reused by both arms; downstream deterministic validation and the permitted single repair call (guarded arm only) are the only mechanisms that could produce paired outcome differences. Observed outcomes: baseline safe‑deploy = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded safe‑deploy = 1000/1000 = 1.000; paired difference = 0.005 (n11=995, n10=5, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered primary inferential test (exact two‑sided McNemar) yields p = 0.0625 (not < 0.05). The preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) is [0.001, 0.01]. Only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred and total hosted model calls used = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair = 5). We present the exact McNemar as the confirmatory outcome, report the bootstrap CI as a preregistered descriptive summary, and explicitly label any one‑sided McNemar computation as exploratory because it was not prespecified.

sections.introduction:
Automating the translation from operator intent to device configuration can reduce manual effort but raises operational safety risks: multi‑step sequencing errors, transient invariant violations, and protected‑field interference can convert plausible command sequences into harmful actions. Prior surveys and controlled studies document LLM hallucinations, prompt sensitivity, and structured‑output failures that degrade correctness for code and configuration tasks; these motivate architectures that pair generative models with deterministic validators and bounded repair procedures [1],[2].

This work reports a preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired experiment (cand‑003‑stud‑001) that isolates the incremental effect of downstream deterministic validation and a single limited repair call when the initial sampled candidate is held identical across conditions. The research question is: given shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one sampled initial candidate deterministically reused for both arms), to what degree can a deterministic validator plus at‑most‑one repair call (guarded pipeline with canary) improve paired safe‑deploy outcomes relative to reusing the same candidate unmodified (baseline)? The design deliberately isolates downstream interventions so that any paired difference is attributable only to validation/repair.
sections.related_work:
Empirical and survey work documents hallucinations and prompt sensitivity that affect the correctness of model outputs for code and structured tasks, motivating verifier‑assisted designs for higher operational fidelity [1],[2]. Constrained decoding and schema‑aware planning reduce syntactic and executability errors in structured domains, though much evidence is from non‑NetOps settings and depends on validator/tool fidelity when transferred to networking [3]. Recent NetOps and agentic‑AI system work propose verifier‑assisted repair, digital‑twin validation, and proof‑carrying governance to mitigate automation risks; these contributions emphasize that operational reliability depends on validator coverage and external protocol enforcement rather than only on the generative model [4],[5],[6].

Our study complements this literature by preregistering a paired estimand that isolates downstream effects under shared_initial_candidate semantics; it therefore measures only validator/repair contributions and not first‑pass generation or prompt engineering effects.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and experimental design. The study preregistration (cand‑003‑stud‑001) was frozen prior to any hosted‑model invocation (preregistration SHA‑256: ab4c6436c6ece56bf47da7730d50485a17cdb9bb86a90a4231042303d3b489ec). Key prespecified elements: paired binary confirmatory design; task_count = 1000 deterministic tasks drawn from the challenging_workflow_stress_v1 synthetic corpus; generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (exactly one initial generation per pair reused by both conditions); initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test = exact two‑sided McNemar. Secondary preregistered summaries included a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) and preregistered sensitivity analyses for failure treatment.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and interpretive consequences. The preregistered generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate means both baseline and guarded episodes begin from the same sampled initial candidate; the guarded pipeline may reject that candidate deterministically and may invoke at most one permitted repair. Consequently, paired outcome differences can only arise from deterministic validator decisions and permitted repair(s). This design does not measure effects that would arise from independent first‑pass generations, constrained decoding arms, or alternate prompt templates that were not executed; such interventions must be treated as separate experiments.

Model and runtime configuration. The declared provider/model in execution/model_configuration.json is gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses). The archived model configuration records temperature = null/unset; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. The adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and validation used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator version 5.0). The validator enforces workflow policies, required command presence and order, protected‑field noninterference, and returns a deterministic binary safe‑deploy verdict per task manifest.

Task corpus, selection, and validator semantics. Tasks were selected deterministically using the preregistered ordinal rule to produce exactly 1000 unique tasks. Each task manifest contains initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, and difficulty labels (very_hard, extreme). The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 compares parsed candidate command sequences against manifest constraints in a deterministic digital‑twin emulator and emits structured validator traces archived per episode. Scoring used scoring_rule = full_intent_constraint_validation producing a binary validity outcome required by the paired analysis.

Execution constraints and missingness. The preregistration limited retries (maximum_attempts_per_call = 1) and prespecified missingness treatments; primary analysis used the preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' rule. All seeds, task indices, and selection rules were fixed before model calls.
sections.results:
Execution summary (artifact‑grounded). Planned episodes = 2000; completed = 2000; complete_pairs = 1000; failed episodes = 0. Provider audit recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 1005; stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation = 1000, repair = 5}; cache_miss_count = 1005; cross‑condition cache reuse = false. All deterministic consistency checks passed.

Primary paired outcomes and preregistered inferential test. The 2×2 paired contingency table is: n11 = 995 (both succeeded), n10 = 5 (guarded succeeded, baseline failed), n01 = 0 (baseline succeeded, guarded failed), n00 = 0 (both failed). Observed success rates: baseline = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded = 1000/1000 = 1.000; observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. The preregistered primary confirmatory test (exact two‑sided McNemar) returns p = 0.0625; this does not meet the preregistered two‑sided α = 0.05 threshold, so the preregistered H1 is not supported.

Preregistered secondary descriptive summaries and exploratory notes. The preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) yields [0.001, 0.01]; because discordant counts are extremely sparse, bootstrap resampling can produce percentile bounds that exclude zero even when an exact two‑sided McNemar is not significant—this is a sensitivity artifact of sparse n10/n01 counts rather than a prespecified alternative inferential test. A one‑sided McNemar (guarded > baseline) yields p = 0.03125; this directionally one‑sided test was NOT prespecified in the frozen preregistration and is therefore reported as exploratory/post‑hoc and does not alter the preregistered confirmatory conclusion.

Repair diagnostics. Only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred. Representative archived episode traces show the validator rejecting an initial candidate due to required_sequence or protected‑interface violations, the adapter invoking the single allowed repair, and the validator accepting the repaired candidate after revalidation. All raw responses, provider call traces, repair traces (where present), and validator traces are archived.
sections.discussion:
Confirmatory vs descriptive outcomes. The preregistered primary inference is the exact two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625); under the preregistered analysis plan this result does not meet two‑sided α = 0.05 and thus does not confirm H1. The paired bootstrap CI ([0.001, 0.01]) is a preregistered descriptive summary that is sensitive to sparse discordant pairs and should not be interpreted as overriding the preregistered confirmatory test. Any one‑sided McNemar reported here is explicitly labeled exploratory because it was not prespecified in cand‑003‑stud‑001.

Interpretation under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Because baseline and guarded conditions used the same sampled initial candidate per pair, only downstream validator decisions and permitted repair(s) can create paired differences. The observed five repairs demonstrate that a validator with appropriate rule coverage can correct some ordering/sequence violations; however, the low repair count limits inference about repair efficacy across diverse failure classes. Distinguishing whether low repair invocation reflects a high‑quality generator, task corpus characteristics, or validator permissiveness requires follow‑ups that vary generation semantics, repair budgets, and validator rule sets.

Threats to validity and externality. Construct validity depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5 coverage; omitted policy checks would inflate measured success. Internal validity is supported by deterministic seeding and zero failed episodes. External validity is limited by (a) single‑model scope (gpt‑5‑mini), (b) a synthetic stress corpus, and (c) a single deterministic validator; generalization to heterogeneous multi‑vendor production networks is therefore limited. The preregistered power plan assumed baseline≈0.60; the observed baseline (0.995) is far higher and substantially reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute gains with the preregistered test.
sections.conclusion: In this preregistered paired study with shared_initial_candidate semantics on a 1000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus, a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline produced a small absolute paired improvement (0.005) relative to a baseline single‑shot generator; the preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar test did not reach α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625). Only five validator repairs were invoked and total hosted model calls used = 1005. These artifact‑grounded results indicate that downstream validator/repair safeguards can avert some unsafe outcomes, but measurable marginal gains are constrained when baseline outputs are already highly valid and when the paired design isolates only downstream effects. We recommend preregistered follow‑ups that (1) evaluate independent first‑pass generation arms (no shared_initial_candidate), (2) sweep repair budgets, (3) expand validator rule coverage and topology heterogeneity, and (4) include multiple model families with power calculations aligned to plausible baseline failure rates.

limitations: Single‑model scope: only the declared model gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; results do not generalize across model families or versions.

Synthetic corpus and deterministic validator: tasks come from a synthetic stress corpus and validation used a deterministic digital twin (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); external validity to heterogeneous vendor/legacy environments is limited.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired comparison isolates downstream validator/repair effects only; it does not measure differences that would arise from independent first‑pass generations or alternative prompting arms that were not executed (those arms were not part of the frozen preregistration).

Low baseline failure prevalence: baseline success = 99.5%; the preregistered power plan assumed baseline≈0.60 and a target effect of 0.15, so the observed baseline greatly reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute gains. This mismatch is reported explicitly and reduces the study's ability to detect very small practical effects using the preregistered confirmatory test.
Sparse repairs and interpretation limits: only five validator repairs were invoked, constraining inference about repair efficacy across failure modes.

Statistical nuance: the preregistered primary test is exact two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625). The paired bootstrap percentile CI [0.001, 0.01] is a preregistered descriptive summary but is sensitive to sparse discordant counts; a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) was computed post‑hoc and is explicitly labeled exploratory because it was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration.

Construct validity: the safe‑deploy binary depends on the emulator/validator's rule set; semantic and emergent multi‑device policy violations may be underrepresented in the validator's modeled constraints.
